$comment: T-3578 format, the smooth style (T-3696; docs/AUDIO.md § Narration style): the same words as the panel shows, with ElevenLabs v3 audio tags in square brackets and [short pause]/[long pause] and ellipses for pauses, a pause at each change of subject, no whispering, at most one laugh. Performance only: a tone is a reading, not evidence of how anyone spoke (L-jaunt-voices-3578). Keyed <part>:<id>.

scripts.opening:opening:
[measured] Second Empire style walk.

[short pause] A spring sunset, 1904. The mansard roof came from Paris: a steep slope that hides a whole extra storey, crowned with iron cresting and pierced with dormers. [short pause] By the 1880s it dominated the street, and the Glessner House Museum calls it Prairie Avenue's most popular style.

[short pause] Six houses on foot, 1620 to 2115 Prairie, north to south: a pioneer's roof that swells into a crown, Pullman's palace, a house that bought a mansard to keep up with the neighbours, the street's last survivor, the richest man in Chicago, and the meatpacker's widow. [short pause] Watch the sunset catch the slate.

[short pause] Start at 1620, with a roof drawn for a magazine in 1874.
scripts.stop:law: [measured] 1620 Prairie, Robert Law's house, engraved in 1874 for a series on the homes of Chicago: two storeys over a raised basement under a slated mansard with round-headed dormers, its north part rising into a taller curved crown. [short pause] Compare the drawing's roof with the one in front of you, then walk a block south to the grandest mansard on the street.
scripts.stop:pullman: [measured] 1729 Prairie, George Pullman's house of 1870 to 1876, read by the district register as a brownstone block under a mansard with dormers and iron cresting, entered by a portico on Prairie Avenue. [short pause] Inside: a theatre of about two hundred seats, a pipe organ and a bowling alley, and later a palm room and a large conservatory by Solon S. Beman. Pullman died in 1897; his widow still keeps it. It is razed in 1922. [short pause] Across Eighteenth Street, a smaller house that refused to be left behind.
scripts.stop:jones: [measured] 1834 Prairie, Fernando Jones's house, built in 1866 as an Italianate house with a low roof. [short pause] Twenty years later his neighbours all had mansards. In 1886 the house 'received a mansard addition to bring it into fashion with many of its neighbors': a whole new top storey, bought to keep up. [short pause] That is how a style takes over a street. The hat comes off for good in 1942, when the house is razed. [short pause] Two doors south stands the one Second Empire house that will outlive them all.
scripts.stop:e-keith: [measured] 1900 Prairie, Elbridge G. Keith's house of 1870, by John W. Roberts. [short pause] The district marker calls it 'The last surviving example of the popular Second Empire style, which dominated the street by the 1880s.' Keith was a bank president, and his house will still be standing long after the palaces around it are gone. [short pause] Look for the slate mansard over the corner bay, then cross the avenue to the biggest fortune of all.
scripts.stop:field: [measured] 1905 Prairie, Marshall Field's house, by Richard Morris Hunt, read by the district register as a broad brick and stone mansion under a mansard, with an angular corner bay, dormers and a central portico. [short pause] Field, 'the wealthiest and most powerful businessman in Chicago', lived here. Picture his carriage turning in at sunset; the house will be razed in 1955. [short pause] One more mansard, at the far end of the row.
scripts.stop:armour: [measured] 2115 Prairie, the Kelley-Armour house of 1871, which the district marker calls a stately Second Empire residence: a patterned slate mansard with cresting over a central arched doorway under a pediment. [short pause] Built for the lumberman David Kelley, it became the home of the meatpacker Philip D. Armour, who boasted of using 'everything but the squeal'. His widow still lives here, and will be among the street's last residents. [short pause] The house is razed ten years after her death, in 1937.
scripts.ending:finish:
[measured] End of the Second Empire walk. Count the mansards you passed: by the 1880s they lined the street, and even old houses bought them.

[short pause] Then taste changed, the families moved north, and most of these roofs came down. Only Elbridge Keith's survives. [short pause] Go back and look at it again before the light goes.
